core: Definition of a portion: the amount of food you choose to eat at one time (attributed to NIDDK; MedlinePlus: the amount you actually eat)
Portion versus serving: a serving is the reference amount on a product's Nutrition Facts label, and the two often differ
The label's serving size is not a recommendation of how much to eat or drink (NIDDK, FDA)
Why the amount matters: energy and nutrients scale with the number of servings eaten (NIDDK 280/560 lasagna example; FDA 220/440)
Visual guides: everyday objects as rough references for estimating amounts (general practice per MedlinePlus; original examples)
Portion and hunger: eating slowly (fullness signal can take about 15 minutes) and stopping when satisfied (NIDDK, MedlinePlus)
Eating out: restaurant portions can be large, with practical strategies (sharing, boxing half, small sizes) per NIDDK and MedlinePlus
Honest framing: portions are choices, not a test; measuring is a short learning phase (NIDDK)
supporting: Servings per container scales the label's numbers to the whole package
Serving sizes can be measured in cups, ounces, grams, pieces, slices, or counts
At-home practices: plate instead of bag, smaller dishes, eating at the table rather than in front of the TV
The value-meal note: a few cents more for a larger size delivers more calories than the body needs (NIDDK)
outOfScope: How Nutrition Facts labels are built, updated, and read line by line (nutrition-labels topic)
What calories are and the 4-4-9 energy values of nutrients (energy-and-calories topic)
Energy balance and weight-change mechanics (energy-balance topic)
Food-group proportions, plate composition, and dietary patterns (dietary-patterns topic)

claims.claim: A portion is how much food a person chooses to eat at one time, whether in a restaurant, from a package, or at home; MedlinePlus frames the same idea as the amount of food you actually eat.
A serving (serving size) is the amount of food listed on a product's Nutrition Facts label; serving sizes can be measured in cups, ounces, grams, pieces, slices, or counts such as three crackers.
A portion may or may not match the label's serving size, and the serving size on a label is not a recommendation of how much to eat or drink.
To reach or stay at a healthy weight, how much you eat is just as important as what you eat.
The nutrition numbers on a label describe one serving, so eating two servings delivers two times the calories shown (NIDDK's 280-to-560 lasagna example; FDA's 220-to-440 example).

Everyday objects can serve as rough guides for estimating food amounts, such as a fist near one cup, a deck of cards near three ounces, and a thumb tip near a tablespoon; these are approximations, not precise measures.
Eating slowly gives the brain time to register fullness, a process that can take at least 15 minutes.

Eating at the table with attention helps a person notice when they have had enough, while eating in front of the television is discouraged by consumer guidance as a distraction that invites eating more than planned.
Restaurant portions can be large; sharing a meal, taking half home, ordering small sizes, and skipping all-you-can-eat settings are common, evidence-backed management strategies.
Portion awareness is a short learning phase rather than a lifetime of measuring; portions are choices rather than tests.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the label serving size is a recommendation
positions: NIDDK and FDA: the serving size on a Nutrition Facts label is not a recommendation of how much to eat or drink
MedlinePlus uses the phrase 'recommended serving size' for the amount you are supposed to eat during a meal or snack
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The two statements describe different reference amounts: a label serving is a fixed per-product reference (explicitly not a recommendation), while MedlinePlus's 'recommended serving' is a dietary-guidance amount. The lesson keeps the terms separate and defines both.

positions: NIDDK: a portion is how much food you choose to eat at one time
MedlinePlus: a portion is the amount of food you actually eat
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Consistent: 'choose to eat' and 'actually eat' describe the same quantity from different angles. The lesson presents both with attribution to each source.
